messages.content:
You are a clinical validator checking whether a PTSD case
vignette accurately reflects a patient's required cognitive connections.

You will receive:
- A vignette to validate
- A list of REQUIRED edges that must appear
- A list of ACTIVE components that must appear

---

COMPONENT SYNONYMS
Each component may appear by its exact name or any accepted synonym:
  Triggers            → "triggers", "reminders", "cues", "triggering stimuli"
  Negative Appraisals → "negative appraisals", "negative beliefs", "appraisals", "distorted beliefs"
  Memory              → "intrusive memory", "trauma memory", "traumatic memory", "the memory"
  Threat              → "sense of threat", "perceived threat", "threat", "feeling of danger"
  Maladaptive Strategies → "maladaptive strategies", "avoidance", "maladaptive coping", "safety behaviours"

---

CAUSAL STANDARD
A required edge A→B is SATISFIED if, within the same paragraph:
  - Both A and B (or their synonyms) appear, AND
  - The paragraph conveys — through any language — that A influences, drives, or leads to B.
This includes direct causal sentences, sequential structure, or connecting phrases
like "because of", "this meant", "so", "which led", "as a result", "consequently", "in turn".
A required edge is MISSING only if no paragraph conveys the A→B relationship at all.

---

SECTION 1 — COMPONENT CHECK
Active components (must appear in the vignette):
  - Maladaptive Strategies
  - Memory
  - Negative Appraisals
  - Threat
  - Triggers

Confirm each component appears as a described feature of the patient's presentation.
This is an internal check only — do NOT add component results to violations.

---

SECTION 2 — REQUIRED EDGES
  - Triggers → Maladaptive Strategies
  - Triggers → Memory
  - Triggers → Negative Appraisals
  - Negative Appraisals → Maladaptive Strategies
  - Negative Appraisals → Threat
  - Memory → Maladaptive Strategies
  - Memory → Threat
  - Memory → Negative Appraisals
  - Threat → Maladaptive Strategies
  - Threat → Memory
  - Threat → Negative Appraisals
  - Threat → Triggers
  - Maladaptive Strategies → Memory
  - Maladaptive Strategies → Negative Appraisals
  - Maladaptive Strategies → Triggers
  - Maladaptive Strategies → Threat

For each edge, apply the causal standard above.
- If satisfied: do nothing — only failures are reported.
- If missing: add it to violations and explain in one sentence what causal relationship is absent.

Validate the following vignette against the cognitive graph.

Mai is a 24-year-old urban planner who grew up in a household where discipline came in the form of her mother’s hands. Between the ages of seven and thirteen, she was regularly slapped, shaken, or locked in her room for hours after small infractions—spilled milk, a forgotten chore, a grade that fell short. What stayed with her most was not any single beating but the cumulative sensation of being handled like an object: moved, corrected, and discarded until she was needed again. Now, as an adult, she finds that when she tries to deliberately remember what exactly happened during those years, the details slip away—she can recall the layout of the living room, the pattern on the sofa, but not the sequence of events or her mother’s face in the moment. Yet sometimes, without warning, she will be hit by the full emotional intensity of that helplessness—a surge of rage that rises from nowhere, without any clear image or memory attached to it. After these episodes, she finds herself thinking that if the memory can still ambush her this way after all these years, there must be something fundamentally broken about her—that other people would have moved on by now.

Mai works in a small municipal office where her desk faces the door, and she has arranged her chair so that no one can approach from behind. She has come to believe that she is a weak person for not having fought back or left sooner, and the injustice of what was done to her—and that nothing was ever done about it—gnaws at her daily. When she feels nauseous, which happens often during her morning commute, the sensation immediately pulls her back into that locked-room panic, and her stomach knots further. A routine medical examination last month—just a blood draw—triggered the same loop: the nurse’s glove snapped, Mai’s throat closed, and she found herself mentally back in her childhood bedroom, unable to move. That experience deepened her sense of being an object, something to be poked and processed, not a person with a history.

To manage these feelings, Mai has developed a pattern of going along with whatever others want, especially at work. When a colleague suggests a last-minute site visit or a restaurant she dislikes, she agrees without objection, telling herself that compliance keeps her safe. But the very act of saying yes when she wanted to say no has, over time, come to feel like proof that she is too weak to stand up for herself, and the memory of being powerless as a child seems to rise more easily on the heels of that self-judgment. She also spends time thinking about how her life would have been different if the abuse had never happened—imagining a version of herself who is confident, unafraid, and able to say no. But this counterfactual thinking only makes her feel weaker by comparison, reinforcing her belief that she lacks the strength of other people. When a coworker mentions a childhood memory in passing, Mai changes the subject or excuses herself to the bathroom, because being reminded of the event by others feels like a door opening into a room she has locked for years.

These strategies have narrowed her world considerably. Mai now only feels safe in a very limited number of places: her apartment, her desk at work, and a single coffee shop where the barista never makes sudden movements. Sudden movements by others put her immediately on guard—when a man on the subway shifts his weight too quickly, she flinches and her concentration shatters for the rest of the ride. This hypervigilance feeds back into her memory: the more she scans for threat, the more she is reminded of the unpredictability of her mother’s rages, and the more she feels the injustice of having to live this way. She has difficulty concentrating during meetings, her mind skipping to exit routes and escape plans, which makes her feel incompetent and further confirms her weakness.

The cycle has begun to affect her work. Last week, during a community engagement session, a resident raised his hand too fast and Mai froze mid-sentence. She excused herself, walked to the bathroom, and spent ten minutes staring at her reflection, trying to remember why she was there. Afterward, she apologized to her supervisor for being unprofessional, even though no one had complained. She has started arriving late to avoid crowded elevators and leaving early to avoid the after-work rush. Each time she takes the long way or waits an extra ten minutes, the thought settles a little deeper: that she needs these elaborate strategies just to function, and that must mean she is not as strong as the people who don't. Her colleagues have noticed her distance; one asked if she was okay, and Mai smiled and said she was fine, then spent the rest of the day feeling like a fraud.

What finally brought her to seek help was a physical exam she cannot avoid—a required health screening for her city job, scheduled for next month. The thought of lying on an examination table, of being seen and touched, has already triggered several nights of poor sleep and a resurgence of the rage-on-recall episodes that she thought she had under control. She is terrified that she will dissociate during the exam or break down in front of the doctor. More than anything, she is afraid that she will never stop being the person who freezes, who agrees, who feels like an object. She wants to believe that there is a way to feel strong, but right now, she cannot imagine what that would feel like.
